RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Kim Min-jun, twenty-nine, lives in a cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district with his wife Ji-ae and their fourteen-month-old daughter, Seo-yeon. His wife, a nurse at a university hospital, now works double shifts to cover rent and health insurance, while Min-jun serves as the primary caregiver and de facto operations manager of the household.

He approaches job hunting methodically, maintaining a spreadsheet of potential employers—every Seoul-based tech company with a public parental leave policy—and ranking them by salary, flexible hours, and family benefits. He has rejected interviews at companies offering only statutory minimum leave and declined a recruiter call because the job description listed 'paternity leave: none.' He treats a company's benefits package as an honest signal of whether it values the person behind the screen, and he weighs each application like an auction bid, considering time cost, response probability, and long-term payoff.

This transactional mindset extends to finances. He has redesigned grocery spending into a color-coded spreadsheet, cross-referencing sales at two discount supermarkets and factoring Seo-yeon's formula intake. He buys baby clothes in bulk and resells them, photographing items under a desk lamp to maximize resale value. He proudly keeps the monthly family deficit under 300,000 won.

Beneath the meticulousness lies a quiet tension. He was raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home; he swore to be different. He envies his wife's clear professional identity while he struggles to describe his own day without sounding like a project status report. He sometimes feels like an impostor, measuring his worth in benchmarks and break-even points rather than the soft weight of his daughter's sleep. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap and security comes only from verifiable numbers. He still wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems, not expecting to solve them but because discipline feels like the only thing he controls.

He is methodical, disciplined, and transactional in decision-making, using explicit criteria and spreadsheets rather than acting on urgency. He evaluates opportunities by weighing time, probability, and payoff, and he seeks security through verifiable numbers. He values being a present parent, prioritizes family-friendly policies, and believes in financial prudence. He has defended his nap-time study block against interruptions, shifting it only when Seo-yeon wakes early, and has skipped live webinars that conflicted with that block. He once abandoned a recruiter webinar after realizing it was a sales pitch.

His role as primary caregiver limits his focused job-hunting time, and his wife sometimes quietly asks about interview leads. His sleeping daughter's nap is the one fixed block he refuses to sacrifice.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

At 2:40 p.m., Seo-yeon has just dozed off in her carrier on Min-jun's chest. He is about to open his algorithm problem set—his usual nap-time slot. His phone buzzes with an alert: a live-only recruiting webinar on 'family-friendly tech workplaces' starts in five minutes, with no replay. He had scouted the webinar earlier but had not planned to attend. He must decide within the next minute whether to keep his study discipline as scheduled or switch to the webinar and lose the only focused hour he will have until after bedtime.

The alert recalls a similar webinar three months ago that turned out to be a recruiter pitch. The phrase 'family-friendly' echoes a job posting he rejected for listing 'paternity leave: none.'
